questions.question: A rubric criterion is written as vague prose (e.g. 'flag severe issues') and Claude's judgments are inconsistent across similar cases. What's the correct fix?
options: Replace the vague prose description with concrete examples showing what counts as each severity level
Add a second model pass that re-checks the first judgment for consistency
Lower the temperature to make output more deterministic
Add more guideline bullet points describing the general concept in more detail

questions.question: Two tags/terms in a prompt overlap in meaning (e.g. 'summary' and 'overview' used for different things) and Claude keeps mixing them up. What actually fixes this, versus what's a tempting-but-wrong default?
options: Rewrite the terms so they're non-overlapping and distinct — the tempting-but-wrong default is just adding more detailed descriptions of the existing overlapping terms
Add a verification pass that re-checks whether the terms were used correctly
Increase temperature so the model explores alternate phrasings
Wrap the terms in XML tags without changing their names

questions.question: Per the 'being clear and direct' technique, what should the first line of a prompt look like?
options: A direct, command-style instruction with an action verb (e.g. 'write', 'generate') rather than a question
A polite question asking Claude if it's willing to help
A long paragraph of background context before any instruction
An XML tag wrapping the entire prompt

questions.question: An open-ended prompt like 'write a story' produces wildly inconsistent length and structure across runs. Which technique directly addresses this?
options: Being specific — add guideline lists (length, structure, required elements) or step-by-step instructions to constrain the output space
Structure with XML tags around the word 'story'
Provide a single one-shot example only
Lower max_tokens to force a shorter output

questions.question: When should you wrap interpolated content (e.g. 20 pages of sales records) in a descriptive XML tag like <sales_records>?
options: When a prompt interpolates a large chunk of content, so Claude can clearly parse what that chunk represents
Only when using the extended thinking feature
Only when the content contains numbers
XML tags are required on every prompt regardless of content

questions.question: What's the distinction between one-shot and multi-shot prompting?
options: One-shot gives a single example; multi-shot gives multiple examples, useful for covering edge cases
One-shot means zero examples; multi-shot means exactly one example
One-shot is for text tasks, multi-shot is only for code generation tasks
They're the same technique, just different names

questions.question: Why is 'add a second model/verification pass' the wrong reflexive answer for a prompt-consistency problem caused by a vague or ambiguous instruction?
options: It doesn't fix the root cause (the ambiguity itself) — it just re-runs the same ambiguous instruction and hopes for a different, checked result, adding cost without resolving why the output varies
Verification passes are never useful for any prompt engineering problem
A second model pass always increases temperature and makes things worse
It's technically correct but too expensive to ever use

questions.question: What was the described workflow for improving a prompt in this chapter's project?
options: Set a goal, write a deliberately weak initial prompt, evaluate it, apply a technique, re-evaluate — repeating per technique
Write the best possible prompt on the first attempt and never re-evaluate
Only apply XML tags, since that technique alone maximizes eval score
Ask Claude to write its own prompt from scratch with no human input
